implementation_notes: JSON is JavaScript's own object notation, so the serializer is the built-in JSON.stringify/JSON.parse pair and the LOB is a TEXT/JSON/JSONB column (node:sqlite binds the string directly, other drivers accept objects when configured). The classic mapper disappears entirely, and what remains is the deliberate decision about what the payload may contain: JSON drops undefined and function properties, throws on BigInt and cycles, and loses class prototypes and Dates on the way back.
pitfalls: JSON.stringify throws on circular references and BigInt while silently dropping undefined and function properties, so a graph containing any of those needs a replacer or another format.
Dates become ISO strings and Map/Set become {}: revive types explicitly (toJSON plus a reviver) or the graph shape changes across the round trip.
A JSON string in a TEXT column is invisible to indexes; on big graphs the driver and database limits (max_allowed_packet, SQLITE_MAX_LENGTH) become the ceiling.

variants.name: Node v8 structured-clone blob
variants.implementation_notes: node:v8 exposes the structured clone algorithm as v8.serialize/v8.deserialize: the Buffer it returns binds to a BLOB column and preserves Map, Set, Date, RegExp and cyclic references that JSON cannot represent. It is Node-only and version-sensitive, so it fits internal caches and session state, not an interchange format; prefer JSON whenever anything else must read the payload.
pitfalls: The serialized format follows the Node/V8 version, so a blob written by one runtime is not guaranteed to load in another or after a major upgrade.
Deserialization reconstructs arbitrary structures from the stream, so treat stored payloads as trusted data only.
